0.title: The Sound Church: Titus and the Gospel-Ordered Life
0.overview:
Titus is the most compressed of the three Pastoral Epistles — three chapters of extraordinary density that move from theology to character to conduct without pausing. Paul writes to Titus, his Greek co-worker and 'true child in a common faith,' whom he has left on Crete with a single, sprawling assignment: 'put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town' (1:5). The churches of Crete are young, disorganized, and under pressure from teachers who combine Jewish speculative traditions with moral permissiveness. Titus's task is to build a church that looks like the gospel it proclaims.

Crete was one of the ancient world's most storied islands — home to a hundred cities, to the legendary palace of Knossos and the Minoan civilization, and to a reputation for unreliability so notorious it had become proverbial in antiquity. The Cretan philosopher Epimenides (c. 6th century BC) had declared that 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons,' a statement Paul quotes in 1:12 without embarrassment — cultural honesty is not racism, and the false teachers have confirmed the description. Paul and Titus had apparently visited Crete together at some point unrecorded in Acts (probably during the period between Paul's first and second Roman imprisonments), planted churches across the island, and then Paul left Titus to complete the work while he moved on.

The letter's organizing principle is the word 'sound' — hygiainō (healthy, health-giving). Sound doctrine (1:9; 2:1), sound faith (1:13; 2:2), sound speech (2:8) are the letter's repeated standard. The false teachers produce diseased teaching — teaching that makes people spiritually sick. Sound doctrine, by contrast, produces healthy congregations: older men of dignity, older women who form the younger, young people of self-control, slaves whose conduct adorns the gospel. The letter is a sustained argument that right belief and right living are inseparable — that the grace of God which saves also trains; that the gospel is not just good news about forgiveness but the power that produces a 'people for his own possession, eager for good works' (2:14).

Two Christological passages make Titus indispensable for preaching the full person of Christ. In 2:13 the Greek grammar (Sharp's Rule) identifies Jesus Christ as 'our great God and Savior' — one of the New Testament's most explicit affirmations of full deity. In 3:4–7 the paragraph on regeneration, justification, and Spirit-renewal is one of the most complete soteriological statements in Paul's letters, anchoring the call to godly conduct in the deepest possible theological foundation: God saved us not because of what we did but entirely by his own mercy, through the Spirit's renewing, so that we might become heirs of the hope of eternal life. The letter that sounds like a manual of church order is, at its root, a profound meditation on grace.

1.title: The Ordered Church: Elders, Sound Doctrine, and False Teachers
1.overview:
Paul left Titus on Crete to finish organising the young churches. Chapter 1 has three parts: a long greeting that grounds everything in the God who cannot lie (vv. 1–4); the qualifications of elders, who must be men of proven character able to teach and to refute (vv. 5–9); and a sharp word about false teachers, mostly from the circumcision party, who teach for money and whose lives contradict their talk (vv. 10–16).

The parts belong together. The elders are defined by the threat, and the false teachers are exposed by the standard. Truth, Paul insists, “accords with godliness” (v. 1); men who “profess to know God, but … deny him by their works” (v. 16) have failed the test.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, God’s servant and Christ’s apostle, writes for the faith of God’s chosen people and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness, in the hope of eternal life promised by God, who cannot lie, before time began, and now revealed through the preaching entrusted to Paul. He greets Titus, his true son in their shared faith, with grace and peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
The God Who Cannot Lie, Writing to Crete

Apseudes, the unlying God (v.2), is the first thing Paul says about God to an island proverbial for lying (v.12); and the eternal promise reaches anyone only through preaching entrusted to a man (v.3).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Titus was the uncircumcised test case at Jerusalem (Gal 2:1-3) and the man sent into the Corinthian crisis (2 Cor 7:6).

Now: Knowledge of the truth is recognised by the godliness it produces (v.1).

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, for the sake of the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness, in hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began and at the proper time manifested in his word through the preaching with which I have been entrusted by the command of God our Savior;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, for the sake of the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness, in hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began and at the proper time manifested in his word through the preaching with which I have been entrusted by the command of God our Savior;

Meaning first. Titus 1 is about order in young churches threatened by false teachers. Paul opens with an unusually full greeting that sums up his ministry: he serves the faith of God’s chosen people and their knowledge of the truth that produces godliness, all resting on the hope of eternal life promised by the God who cannot lie (vv. 1–4). Then he explains why he left Titus in Crete: to finish setting the churches in order and to appoint elders in every town (v. 5). The elders must be above reproach in family life (v. 6) and character, not arrogant, hot-tempered, drunken, violent or greedy, but hospitable, self-controlled, upright and holy; and they must hold firmly to the trustworthy message so that they can teach sound doctrine and refute those who oppose it (vv. 7–9). This was urgent, because many rebellious talkers and deceivers, especially from the circumcision party, were upsetting whole households for money (vv. 10–11). Even a Cretan poet had said Cretans were liars, beasts and gluttons; so Titus must rebuke them sharply, so that they become sound in the faith and stop following Jewish myths and human rules (vv. 12–14). To the pure, all things are pure; but the false teachers, defiled in mind and conscience, claim to know God while denying him by their deeds (vv. 15–16).

Setting and background. Titus was a Greek convert and one of Paul’s trusted troubleshooters. Paul had taken him, uncircumcised, to Jerusalem as a test case for the gospel’s freedom (Galatians 2:1–5). He was sent to Corinth to deal with a crisis and to organise the collection (2 Corinthians 2:13; 7:6–15; 8:6, 16–23). After Paul’s release from his first Roman imprisonment, he and Titus evangelised Crete, and Paul left Titus there to organise the churches, writing this letter around AD 63–65. Later Titus went to Dalmatia (2 Timothy 4:10). Crete is a large island south of Greece. Cretans were present at Pentecost (Acts 2:11), so there may have been believers there before Paul arrived.

Paul, a servant of God. Key words. “Servant” (doulos, slave, bondservant). Only here does Paul call himself “a servant of God” (elsewhere “of Christ”). It places him in line with Moses, David and the prophets (Joshua 1:2; Jeremiah 7:25).

And an apostle of Jesus Christ. Key words. Servant expresses humility; apostle expresses authority.

For the sake of the faith of God’s elect. Key words. “For the sake of” (kata, in accordance with, with a view to). Paul’s apostleship exists to bring God’s elect to faith and to build up their faith. “Elect” (eklektōn, chosen ones). God chose a people; Paul preaches so that they will believe (2 Timothy 2:10; Acts 13:48). Election does not make preaching unnecessary; it guarantees its success.

And their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness. Key words. “Knowledge” (epignōsin, full knowledge). “Accords with godliness” (kat’ eusebeian, leads to godliness). True doctrine and godly life are inseparable, a theme of the whole letter (2:11–14; 3:8). The false teachers had knowledge without godliness (v. 16).

In hope of eternal life. Key words. “Hope” (elpidi, confident expectation). Faith, knowledge and godliness rest on the hope of eternal life (3:7).

Which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began. Key words. “Who never lies” (apseudēs, unlying, truthful), a single word. In sharp contrast with the Cretans, who were proverbial liars (v. 12). God cannot lie (Numbers 23:19; Hebrews 6:18). “Before the ages began” (pro chronōn aiōniōn), as in 2 Timothy 1:9. The promise was made in eternity, within the Trinity: the Father promised eternal life to the elect in Christ, before creation. This is sometimes called the covenant of redemption.

And at the proper time manifested in his word through the preaching. Key words. “At the proper time” (kairois idiois, in his own seasons), as in 1 Timothy 2:6. “Manifested” (ephanerōsen, made visible, revealed). “Preaching” (kērygmati, proclamation). What God promised in eternity, he revealed in history through the preached gospel.

With which I have been entrusted by the command of God our Savior. Key words. “Entrusted” (episteuthēn), as in 1 Timothy 1:11. “God our Savior” (1 Timothy 1:1), a title used six times in this short letter, of the Father (1:3; 2:10; 3:4) and of Christ (1:4; 2:13; 3:6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul preached only to people he knew to be elect. He did not know who they were; he preached to all, knowing God would call his own through it. Nor does “promised before the ages began” mean anyone existed before time; it means God’s saving plan was fixed in eternity.

In a sentence. From Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, sent to bring God’s chosen people to faith and to the knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness, all resting on the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before time began, and which at the time he chose he made known through the message entrusted to me by the command of God our Saviour;

For worship. Praise the God who never lies. Every promise he has made to you in Christ will be kept.
verseByVerse.note: Titus was a Greek convert and one of Paul’s trusted troubleshooters. The letter was probably written between Paul’s two Roman imprisonments, in the mid 60s AD.

verseByVerse.quote: To Titus, my true child in a common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To Titus, my true child in a common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.

To Titus, my true child. Key words. “True” (gnēsiō, genuine, legitimate), as of Timothy (1 Timothy 1:2). Titus was probably converted through Paul. He is Paul’s authorised representative.

In a common faith. Key words. “Common” (koinēn, shared). Paul the Jew and Titus the Gentile share one faith. There is not one faith for Jews and another for Gentiles. This was significant in a church troubled by the circumcision party (v. 10).

Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior. Key words. Here Christ is called “Savior,” just after the Father is called “Savior” (v. 3). The same title is given to both. Christ is the Saviour along with the Father, which places him on the side of deity (2:13).

Textual note. Some later manuscripts add “mercy” (“grace, mercy, and peace”), matching 1 and 2 Timothy. The earlier manuscripts have only “grace and peace.”

What it does not mean. “Common” does not mean ordinary or inferior; it means shared by all believers alike.

In a sentence. To Titus, my genuine son in the faith we share: grace and peace from God the Father and from Christ Jesus our Saviour.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for a believer from a very different background who shares your faith. Tell them you are glad of them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–9 — Appointing Elders in Every Town
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul left Titus in Crete to finish organising the churches and appoint elders in every town. An elder must be above reproach, faithful in marriage, with believing children who are not wild or disobedient. As God’s steward an overseer must not be arrogant, quick-tempered, a drunkard, violent or greedy, but hospitable, a lover of good, sensible, just, holy and self-controlled. He must hold firmly to the trustworthy message as taught, so that he can encourage others with sound teaching and correct those who oppose it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Elder and Overseer Are One Office

‘Elders’ (v.5) and ‘overseer’ (v.7) name one office within a single sentence; and of the qualifications, eleven concern character and one competence — to instruct and to rebuke (v.9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Congregations existed across Crete without yet being in working order (v.5).

Now: ‘Children are believers’ (v.6) — or ‘faithful’ — asks whether a household is visibly out of control, not whether a father has guaranteed his children's salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: This is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town as I directed you— if anyone is above reproach, the husband of one wife, and his children are believers and not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town as I directed you— if anyone is above reproach, the husband of one wife, and his children are believers and not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination.

This is why I left you in Crete. Key words. Crete is a large island south of Greece. Acts records Paul only passing along its coast as a prisoner (Acts 27:7–13); the work there likely came after his release from his first imprisonment. Crete had about a hundred cities in ancient times; Paul and Titus had planted churches in several but had not finished organising them.

So that you might put what remained into order. Key words. “Put into order” (epidiorthōsē, set right further, straighten out what remains). A medical word for setting a broken bone, or a carpenter’s word for straightening. The churches were real but incomplete. The chief need was proper leadership.

And appoint elders in every town. Key words. “Appoint” (katastēsēs, set in place, put in charge). “Elders” (presbyterous), plural: each town’s church was to have several elders. “In every town”: each local church needed its own leadership (Acts 14:23).

As I directed you. Key words. “Directed” (dietaxamēn, arranged, gave orders). Paul had already given instructions verbally; he now puts them in writing for Titus’s authority.

If anyone is above reproach. Key words. “Above reproach” (anenklētos, unaccused, blameless), as with deacons in 1 Timothy 3:10. The headline qualification, repeated in verse 7.

The husband of one wife. Key words. Faithful in marriage, devoted to one woman (1 Timothy 3:2).

And his children are believers. Key words. “Believers” (pista, faithful, believing, trustworthy). The word can mean either “believing” or “faithful” (trustworthy, well-behaved). Some think it requires that an elder’s children all be professing Christians; others that they be faithful, well-ordered and respectful. The parallel with 1 Timothy 3:4 (“keeping his children submissive”) and the following phrase (“not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination”) suggests the emphasis is on their behaviour: children who are under his authority and are not wild or rebellious. This concerns children still at home.

And not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination. Key words. “Debauchery” (asōtias, wild, reckless living, dissipation; the word used of the prodigal son, Luke 15:13). “Insubordination” (anypotakta, rebellious, unruly). If an elder cannot lead his own household, he cannot lead the church (1 Timothy 3:5).

Where Christians differ: must an elder’s children be converted? Some insist that all an elder’s children must be professing Christians. Verdict: Since conversion is God’s work and not under a father’s control (John 1:13), and the word can mean “faithful” in the sense of trustworthy, it is better to read this as requiring that his children at home be orderly and respectful, not openly wild or rebellious, showing that he leads his household well. A father who has faithfully raised his children and whose child has not yet professed faith is not thereby disqualified, but a household in open disorder would disqualify him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean an elder must be married or have children; it describes how he must behave if he does. Nor does it require that adult children who have left home live in a certain way; the focus is the household under his authority.

In a sentence. The reason I left you in Crete was so that you could put right what was still unfinished and appoint elders in each town as I instructed you. An elder must give no grounds for accusation, be faithful to his wife, and have children who are trustworthy and not open to the charge of wild living or rebellion.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your church’s elders and their families this week. Their homes are under pressure as well as their ministry.
verseByVerse.note: Crete is a large island south of Greece. Acts records Paul only touching at it as a prisoner (Acts 27:7–13); this later work there is not in Acts.

verseByVerse.quote: For an overseer, as God's steward, must be above reproach. He must not be arrogant or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent or greedy for gain, but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For an overseer, as God’s steward, must be above reproach. He must not be arrogant or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent or greedy for gain, but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it.

For an overseer. Key words. “Elder” (v. 5) and “overseer” (episkopon) here describe the same office, used interchangeably within two verses. This is clear evidence that in the New Testament, elders and overseers (bishops) were the same people.

As God’s steward, must be above reproach. Key words. “Steward” (oikonomon, household manager). In a large household, the steward managed the master’s affairs. He was a servant with authority but accountable. The church is God’s household (1 Timothy 3:15); the elder manages it for God, not for himself.

He must not be arrogant. Key words. “Arrogant” (authadē, self-willed, stubborn, insisting on his own way). A man who must always have his way cannot lead God’s household.

Or quick-tempered. Key words. “Quick-tempered” (orgilon, prone to anger, irritable).

Or a drunkard or violent. Key words. As in 1 Timothy 3:3.

Or greedy for gain. Key words. “Greedy for gain” (aischrokerdē, fond of dishonest profit), as with deacons (1 Timothy 3:8). Especially relevant, since the false teachers taught for gain (v. 11).

But hospitable, a lover of good. Key words. “Hospitable” (philoxenon). “Lover of good” (philagathon, loving goodness, good people and good things), the opposite of 2 Timothy 3:3.

Self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. Key words. “Self-controlled” (sōphrona, sensible). “Upright” (dikaion, righteous, just in his dealings with people). “Holy” (hosion, devout toward God). “Disciplined” (enkratē, self-mastered, in control of his desires).

He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught. Key words. “Hold firm” (antechomenon, cling to, hold on against opposition). “Trustworthy word” (pistou logou, reliable message). “As taught” (kata tēn didachēn, in accordance with the teaching): the apostolic doctrine. An elder must be firmly committed to it, not wavering.

So that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine. Key words. “Give instruction” (parakalein, exhort, encourage). “Sound” (hygiainousē, healthy). His positive task: feeding the flock.

And also to rebuke those who contradict it. Key words. “Rebuke” (elenchein, refute, expose, convict). “Contradict” (antilegontas, speak against). His negative task: protecting the flock from wolves. Both are necessary.

What it does not mean. It does not mean elders must be perfect. They are sinners saved by grace. It means their lives show mature, consistent godliness, and their doctrine is sound.

In a sentence. Because an overseer manages God’s household, he must give no grounds for accusation. He must not be self-willed or short-tempered, given to drink, violent or out for dishonest money, but hospitable, a lover of what is good, sensible, fair, devout and self-disciplined. He must hold tightly to the reliable message as it has been taught, so that he can both encourage others with healthy teaching and refute those who oppose it.

On a Tuesday. Which of these qualities does God want to grow in you, whether or not you are a leader? Pick one and pray for it this week.
verseByVerse.note: “Elder” (v. 5) and “overseer” here describe the same office.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Many in Crete, especially some Jewish Christians who insist on circumcision, are unruly talkers and deceivers who are upsetting whole families for the sake of money. Titus must silence them. Paul quotes a Cretan poet’s harsh verdict on his own people as liars and lazy gluttons and says it is accurate, so Titus must correct them firmly so that they become healthy in the faith and stop following Jewish myths and human rules. To the pure, everything is pure, but nothing is pure to those whose minds and consciences are corrupted. They claim to know God but their conduct denies him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Quoting a Pagan, and Agreeing With Him

Paul endorses Epimenides' verdict on Crete (vv.12–13) not as a racial claim but as the island's own accurate self-assessment — and rebukes sharply so that the offenders ‘may be sound in the faith’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Deceivers overturning whole households must be silenced (v.11), while the deceived are handled gently (2 Tim 2:25).

Now: ‘To the pure all things are pure’ (v.15) abolishes ritual defilement, not sin.

verseByVerse.quote: For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party. They must be silenced, since they are upsetting whole families by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party. They must be silenced, since they are upsetting whole families by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach.

For there are many who are insubordinate. Key words. “For” explains why sound elders were urgent. “Many”: not a few. “Insubordinate” (anypotaktoi, rebellious, refusing to submit), the same word as verse 6. They would not submit to apostolic authority.

Empty talkers and deceivers. Key words. “Empty talkers” (mataiologoi, idle talkers, speakers of nonsense), as in 1 Timothy 1:6. “Deceivers” (phrenapatai, mind-deceivers, seducers of the mind).

Especially those of the circumcision party. Key words. “Of the circumcision” (hoi ek tēs peritomēs): Jewish Christians (or those influenced by them) who insisted on circumcision and the law of Moses, as in Galatia (Galatians 2:12; Acts 15:1, 5). There was a large Jewish community on Crete. Their teaching mixed Jewish myths, purity rules and speculation (v. 14; 3:9).

They must be silenced. Key words. “Silenced” (epistomizein, muzzled, have their mouths stopped, as with a horse’s bridle). Not by force, but by refuting them with sound doctrine (v. 9) and by refusing them a teaching platform in the church.

Since they are upsetting whole families. Key words. “Upsetting” (anatrepousin, overturning), as in 2 Timothy 2:18. “Whole families” (holous oikous, entire households). Churches met in homes; false teaching could overturn a household’s faith and thus a whole house church.

By teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach. Key words. “Shameful gain” (aischrou kerdous, dishonest profit). They taught for money (1 Timothy 6:5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jewish believers were the problem as such; Paul himself was Jewish. The problem was teaching that added the law to Christ. Nor does “silenced” mean persecution or civil punishment; it means refutation and exclusion from teaching in the church.

In a sentence. There are many rebellious people, empty talkers and deceivers, especially among those who insist on circumcision. They must be stopped, because they are overturning entire households by teaching things they should not teach, for the sake of shameful profit.

On a Tuesday. Watch out for teachers who make money central. Support those who teach the gospel faithfully, and be wary of those who peddle it.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said, "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons." This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith,
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.” This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith,

One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said. Key words. The line is usually traced to Epimenides, a Cretan poet-prophet of the sixth century BC, who was regarded by Greeks as a seer. Paul calls him a “prophet” in the sense the Cretans themselves used, not claiming that he was a true prophet of God. Paul also quoted Greek poets in Athens (Acts 17:28) and Corinth (1 Corinthians 15:33).

Cretans are always liars. Key words. Cretans had a reputation for lying. The Greek verb “to Cretanise” (krētizein) meant to lie. One reason: Cretans claimed to have the tomb of Zeus, whom other Greeks thought immortal. The contrast with God “who never lies” (v. 2) is pointed.

Evil beasts. Key words. “Evil beasts” (kaka thēria, wild, dangerous animals): savage, brutal.

Lazy gluttons. Key words. “Lazy gluttons” (gasteres argai, idle bellies): people driven by their appetites, unwilling to work.

This testimony is true. Key words. Paul agrees that it describes the false teachers well: they lie, they are brutal in upsetting families, and they are driven by greed.

Therefore rebuke them sharply. Key words. “Rebuke” (elenche, refute, convict). “Sharply” (apotomōs, severely, cuttingly, abruptly; the word is used of cutting off). The situation called for decisive correction, not gentle persuasion alone. Contrast 2 Timothy 2:25, where gentleness is urged; the method depends on the person and situation.

That they may be sound in the faith. Key words. “Sound” (hygiainōsin, healthy). The goal of the sharp rebuke is restoration, not destruction. “Them” probably refers to the church members who were being influenced, and perhaps the false teachers themselves.

What it does not mean. It does not license ethnic stereotyping of people today. Paul is quoting a Cretan’s self-criticism to describe the false teachers’ character, and Paul’s own aim is that Cretans become sound in the faith; the gospel transforms every people. Nor does quoting a pagan poet mean his words are inspired; Paul’s use of them is inspired, as a true observation.

In a sentence. One of their own, a Cretan whom they regarded as a prophet, said, “Cretans are always liars, savage beasts, idle bellies.” That description is accurate. So rebuke them severely, so that they may be healthy in the faith,

On a Tuesday. What sins is your culture known for? Ask God to make you different, and to use the gospel to transform your community.
verseByVerse.note: The line is usually traced to Epimenides, a Cretan poet-prophet of about 600 BC.

verseByVerse.quote: not devoting themselves to Jewish myths and the commands of people who turn away from the truth. To the pure, all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; but both their minds and their consciences are defiled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
not devoting themselves to Jewish myths and the commands of people who turn away from the truth. To the pure, all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; but both their minds and their consciences are defiled.

Not devoting themselves to Jewish myths. Key words. “Devoting themselves” (prosechontes, paying attention to), as in 1 Timothy 1:4. “Jewish myths” (Ioudaïkois mythois): speculative stories and legends drawn from Jewish tradition, not Scripture itself.

And the commands of people who turn away from the truth. Key words. “Commands of people” (entolais anthrōpōn, human rules). Jesus condemned the same thing (Mark 7:7–8, quoting Isaiah 29:13). Probably purity rules about food and ritual washing, as the next verse suggests (Colossians 2:20–23).

To the pure, all things are pure. Key words. “Pure” (kathara, clean). Purity is a matter of the heart, not of external rules. For those whose hearts have been cleansed by faith (Acts 15:9), no food or created thing is defiling in itself (Mark 7:15, 19; Romans 14:14, 20; 1 Timothy 4:4).

But to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure. Key words. “Defiled” (memiammenois, stained, polluted). “Unbelieving” (apistois). To those whose hearts are unclean, everything they touch is defiled, because the defilement is in them. Ritual rules cannot make them clean.

But both their minds and their consciences are defiled. Key words. “Minds” (nous, thinking, reasoning). “Consciences” (syneidēsis, moral awareness). Both are corrupted. Their thinking is twisted, and their moral compass is broken (1 Timothy 4:2). The problem is not what they eat, but who they are.

What it does not mean. “To the pure, all things are pure” does not mean that nothing is sinful for a believer, or that a pure person can do anything. Paul is speaking of created things like food, not of sin. Sin remains sin. Nor does it mean a believer should ignore a weaker brother’s conscience (Romans 14:13–21).

In a sentence. and will no longer pay attention to Jewish legends or to the rules of people who reject the truth. Everything is clean to those whose hearts are clean, but to those who are corrupted and do not believe, nothing is clean, because their very minds and consciences are polluted.

On a Tuesday. Are you more focused on external rules than on a clean heart? Ask God to cleanse your mind and conscience through Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works. They are detestable, disobedient, unfit for any good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works. They are detestable, disobedient, unfit for any good work.

They profess to know God. Key words. “Profess” (homologousin, confess, claim openly). They claimed special knowledge of God, perhaps through their myths and rules.

But they deny him by their works. Key words. “Deny” (arnountai, disown, renounce). Their lives contradict their claims (2 Timothy 3:5; 1 John 2:4). What we do reveals what we really believe. The test of knowing God is obedience (Matthew 7:16–23; James 2:14–26).

They are detestable. Key words. “Detestable” (bdelyktoi, abominable, disgusting). The word is related to the Old Testament term for an abomination to God. Ironically, they were obsessed with avoiding what was impure; yet they themselves were abominable.

Disobedient. Key words. “Disobedient” (apeitheis, refusing to be persuaded, rebellious).

Unfit for any good work. Key words. “Unfit” (adokimoi, failing the test, disqualified, worthless), as in 2 Timothy 3:8. “Good work” (ergon agathon). A theme of Titus: believers must be devoted to good works (2:7, 14; 3:1, 8, 14). The false teachers were useless for them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean good works save. Paul teaches clearly that we are saved not by works but by mercy (3:5). But true saving faith always produces good works (Ephesians 2:10). A profession of faith with no good works is empty.

In a sentence. They claim to know God, but by the way they live they disown him. They are repulsive, rebellious, and no use for anything good.

On a Tuesday. Does your life confirm or contradict your profession of faith? Choose one good work to do this week that shows you know God.

He must not be arrogant or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent or greedy for gain,<sup>8</sup>but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined.<sup>9</sup>He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it.<sup>10</sup>For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party.<sup>11</sup>They must be silenced, since they are upsetting whole families by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach.<sup>12</sup>One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said, "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons."<sup>13</sup>This testimony is true. They are detestable, disobedient, unfit for any good work.

2.title: Adorning the Doctrine: The Gospel-Shaped Community
2.overview:
Paul tells Titus how each group in the church should live: older men, older women, younger women, younger men, Titus himself, and slaves. Each instruction carries a missionary reason: so that God’s word is not slandered (v. 5), so that opponents have nothing bad to say (v. 8), so that slaves “adorn the doctrine of God our Savior” (v. 10). Ordinary conduct in ordinary roles makes the gospel look like what it is.

Then the reason underneath it all (vv. 11–14). The grace of God has appeared in Christ, and that same grace trains us to say no to ungodliness and to live well now, while we wait for the appearing of “our great God and Savior Jesus Christ”, who gave himself to redeem a people eager to do good. Grace saves, and grace trains.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — What Accords With Sound Doctrine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Titus is to teach the way of life that matches healthy doctrine, group by group. Older men should be sober, serious, wise and sound in faith, love and perseverance. Older women should live reverently, avoid slander and drink, and teach what is good, especially to the younger women, encouraging them to love their husbands and children, live sensibly and purely, manage their homes, be kind and support their husbands, so that God’s word is not brought into disrepute. Young men should be self-controlled. Titus must model good works and serious, sound teaching that opponents cannot fault. Slaves should be dependable and honest with their masters, so that their lives make the teaching about God our Saviour attractive.
verseByVerse.theology:
Doctrine Has a Shape

Titus is to teach what accords with sound doctrine (v.1) — its natural clothing — and the climax is slaves adorning the doctrine of God our Saviour (v.10), the jewel shown to best advantage by the honesty of people with nothing to gain.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The only reason given for the household instructions is missionary: ‘that the word of God may not be reviled’ (v.5).

Now: Older women are commanded to teach (vv.3–4), which bypasses Titus entirely.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for you, teach what accords with sound doctrine. Older men are to be sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled, sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as for you, teach what accords with sound doctrine. Older men are to be sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled, sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness.

Meaning first. Titus 2 shows what sound doctrine looks like when it is lived out in a church, and why. In contrast with the false teachers, whose lives denied God (1:16), Titus must teach what fits healthy doctrine (v. 1). Paul then goes through the household of faith group by group: older men are to be steady, dignified and sound in faith, love and endurance (v. 2); older women are to be reverent, not gossips or drinkers, and to teach what is good (v. 3), training younger women to love their husbands and children, to be sensible, pure, diligent at home, kind and submissive to their husbands, so that God’s word is not discredited (vv. 4–5); younger men are to be self-controlled, and Titus himself must model good works and teach with integrity (vv. 6–8); slaves are to serve faithfully and honestly so as to make the doctrine of God our Saviour attractive (vv. 9–10). Then comes the foundation of it all, one of the great gospel summaries in the New Testament (vv. 11–14): the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation, and it trains us to say no to ungodliness and to live godly lives now, while we wait for the blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, who gave himself to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify a people for his own possession, eager to do good. Titus must teach these things with full authority (v. 15).

But as for you, teach what accords with sound doctrine. Key words. “But as for you” (sy de): in contrast with the false teachers (1:10–16). “Teach” (lalei, speak, keep speaking). “Accords with” (prepei, is fitting, suitable, appropriate). “Sound doctrine” (hygiainousē didaskalia, healthy teaching). Titus is not only to teach doctrine but also the way of life that fits it. Doctrine and life go together.

Older men are to be sober-minded. Key words. “Older men” (presbytas, aged men, probably over fifty or sixty; not the office of elder, which is presbyteros). “Sober-minded” (nēphalious, temperate, clear-headed), as in 1 Timothy 3:2. Age can bring temptations to excess, complacency or bitterness; older men must stay alert.

Dignified. Key words. “Dignified” (semnous, serious, worthy of respect). Their conduct should earn the respect their age deserves.

Self-controlled. Key words. “Self-controlled” (sōphronas, sensible, sound-minded), a keyword of this chapter (vv. 2, 4, 5, 6, 12).

Sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness. Key words. “Sound” (hygiainontas, healthy). Three virtues, like the familiar triad of faith, love and hope (1 Corinthians 13:13), but with steadfastness (hypomonē, patient endurance) in place of hope, since endurance is hope under pressure. Older men must not grow cynical in faith, cold in love, or weary in endurance.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only older men need these qualities; all believers do. Each group is given what it particularly needs. Nor does it suggest older people are past growing.

In a sentence. But you must teach what fits healthy doctrine. Older men should be clear-headed, worthy of respect and sensible, healthy in faith, in love and in endurance.

On a Tuesday. If you are older, ask God to keep you healthy in faith, love and endurance to the end. If you are younger, thank an older believer for their example.

verseByVerse.quote: Older women likewise are to be reverent in behavior, not slanderers or slaves to much wine. They are to teach what is good,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Older women likewise are to be reverent in behavior, not slanderers or slaves to much wine. They are to teach what is good,

Older women likewise are to be reverent in behavior. Key words. “Older women” (presbytidas). “Reverent” (hieroprepeis, fitting for a temple, priest-like, holy in demeanour). Their whole bearing should be like that of someone serving in God’s presence. Their ordinary lives are worship.

Not slanderers. Key words. “Slanderers” (diabolous, accusers, malicious gossips, the word for the devil), as in 1 Timothy 3:11. Older women often know much about family and church life; they must not spread it.

Or slaves to much wine. Key words. “Slaves” (dedoulōmenas, enslaved, perfect tense: in bondage). Drunkenness among older women was a known problem in the ancient world.

They are to teach what is good. Key words. “Teach what is good” (kalodidaskalous, teachers of good, a single compound word). Older women have a vital teaching ministry. Not the public teaching office of elders (1 Timothy 2:12), but a powerful informal ministry, especially to younger women (v. 4), by word and example.

What it does not mean. It does not limit older women’s teaching to these topics only; it highlights a key area. Nor does it mean women cannot teach anyone else; they rightly teach children (2 Timothy 1:5) and may explain the faith in many settings (Acts 18:26).

In a sentence. In the same way, older women should conduct themselves with a reverence fitting for those who serve God, not spreading slander or enslaved to drink. They should be teachers of what is good,

On a Tuesday. Older women: who is a younger woman you could mentor? Invite her for coffee this week.

verseByVerse.quote: and so train the young women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, working at home, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, that the word of God may not be reviled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and so train the young women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, working at home, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, that the word of God may not be reviled.

And so train the young women. Key words. “Train” (sōphronizōsin, teach to be sensible, encourage, bring to their senses), from the same root as “self-controlled.” Older women help younger women to think and live wisely. Titus, a young single man, would not be the best one to do this; the older women would.

To love their husbands and children. Key words. “Love their husbands” (philandrous, husband-loving) and “love their children” (philoteknous, child-loving). Single compound words, using the word for affectionate, warm love (phileō). Love in marriage and parenting does not always come naturally under the strains of daily life; it can and must be learned.

To be self-controlled, pure. Key words. “Self-controlled” (sōphronas, sensible). “Pure” (hagnas, chaste, morally clean, sexually faithful).

Working at home. Key words. “Working at home” (oikourgous, home-workers, busy at home; some manuscripts read oikourous, keepers of the home). Managing the household diligently (1 Timothy 5:14; Proverbs 31:10–31). In contrast with the idle, gossiping younger widows of 1 Timothy 5:13.

Kind. Key words. “Kind” (agathas, good, generous, benevolent).

And submissive to their own husbands. Key words. “Submissive” (hypotassomenas, ordering themselves under, voluntarily yielding). The wife’s voluntary, respectful following of her husband’s loving leadership (Ephesians 5:22–33; Colossians 3:18; 1 Peter 3:1–6). “Their own husbands”: not all men, but one’s own husband.

That the word of God may not be reviled. Key words. “Reviled” (blasphēmētai, slandered, blasphemed). If Christian wives abandoned their families or flouted their husbands, outsiders would blame the gospel. The purpose clause shows the evangelistic motive behind these instructions: making the gospel credible.

Where Christians differ: does this teach a fixed role for wives in every culture? Egalitarians argue that Paul is accommodating to first-century culture to avoid offence, and that in a different culture, mutual submission without distinct roles would better adorn the gospel. Verdict: The motive is indeed partly missional (vv. 5, 8, 10). But elsewhere Paul grounds the wife’s submission in Christ’s relationship with the church (Ephesians 5:22–33) and in creation (1 Corinthians 11:8–9), which do not change with culture. This is the complementarian view: husbands and wives are equal in dignity and worth, with distinct and complementary roles. The husband leads with self-sacrificing love like Christ; the wife follows with respect and strength. This never means a wife must obey a command to sin (Acts 5:29), endure abuse, or lose her voice and gifts.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid women from working outside the home; the excellent wife of Proverbs 31 trades, buys land and sells goods. It means the home is not neglected. Nor does it make submission a matter of inferiority; Christ submitted to the Father, yet is equal with him (1 Corinthians 15:28). And it does not apply to single women, whose calling is equally honourable.

In a sentence. so that they can help the younger women learn to love their husbands and their children, to be sensible and pure, to work hard at home, to be kind, and to follow their own husbands’ lead, so that no one can speak against God’s word.

On a Tuesday. Wives: show your husband one specific act of love and respect this week. Husbands: lead in a way that makes that easy and joyful.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. Show yourself in all respects to be a model of good works, and in your teaching show integrity, dignity, and sound speech that cannot be condemned, so that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. Show yourself in all respects to be a model of good works, and in your teaching show integrity, dignity, and sound speech that cannot be condemned, so that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us.

Likewise, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. Key words. “Urge” (parakalei, exhort, encourage). “Self-controlled” (sōphronein, be sensible, think soundly). Just one quality, but it covers everything: young men are prone to impulsiveness, anger, lust, pride and recklessness. Sound judgement and self-mastery are what they most need (2 Timothy 2:22).

Show yourself in all respects to be a model of good works. Key words. “Show yourself” (seauton parechomenos, presenting yourself). Titus, probably himself a younger man, must teach younger men by example. “Model” (typon, pattern), as in 1 Timothy 4:12. “Good works” (kalōn ergōn), a theme of the letter.

And in your teaching show integrity. Key words. “Integrity” (aphthorian, incorruption, purity, freedom from corrupt motives). Unlike the false teachers who taught for gain (1:11), Titus must teach with pure motives and unadulterated doctrine.

Dignity. Key words. “Dignity” (semnotēta, seriousness, gravity). Treating the things of God with the seriousness they deserve.

And sound speech that cannot be condemned. Key words. “Sound speech” (logon hygiē, healthy word). “Cannot be condemned” (akatagnōston, beyond criticism, unanswerable). His message should be so true and well-grounded that no fair critic can fault it.

So that an opponent may be put to shame. Key words. “Opponent” (ho ex enantias, the one on the opposite side): false teachers or unbelieving critics. “Put to shame” (entrapē, be ashamed, embarrassed). When they look for something to attack and find nothing, they are left ashamed.

Having nothing evil to say about us. Key words. “Us”: Paul includes himself and all believers. A blameless life silences critics (1 Peter 2:12, 15).

What it does not mean. It does not mean critics will never attack; they will. It means our conduct should give them no legitimate grounds.

In a sentence. In the same way, encourage the younger men to be sensible. In everything set them an example by doing good; in your teaching show purity of motive, seriousness, and a healthy message that cannot be faulted, so that anyone who opposes us will be put to shame, having nothing bad to say about us.

On a Tuesday. Younger men: where do you most need self-control? Name it and ask a mature believer to hold you accountable.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants are to be submissive to their own masters in everything; they are to be well-pleasing, not argumentative, not pilfering, but showing all good faith, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bondservants are to be submissive to their own masters in everything; they are to be well-pleasing, not argumentative, not pilfering, but showing all good faith, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior.

Bondservants are to be submissive to their own masters in everything. Key words. “Bondservants” (doulous, slaves). On slavery in the ancient world and Scripture’s response, see 1 Timothy 6:1–2. “In everything”: in all that does not require sin (Acts 5:29).

They are to be well-pleasing. Key words. “Well-pleasing” (euarestous, giving satisfaction). Doing their work well.

Not argumentative. Key words. “Argumentative” (antilegontas, talking back, contradicting), the same word used of false teachers (1:9).

Not pilfering. Key words. “Pilfering” (nosphizomenous, embezzling, secretly keeping back for oneself), the word used of Ananias keeping back part of the money (Acts 5:2–3). Slaves often managed property; petty theft was common and expected.

But showing all good faith. Key words. “Good faith” (pistin agathēn, complete trustworthiness, reliability).

So that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior. Key words. “Adorn” (kosmōsin, decorate, make attractive, arrange beautifully; our word “cosmetic”). The same word used of jewels setting off a beautiful gown. Slaves, the lowest in society, could make the gospel beautiful by their faithful service. The doctrine is already true; their lives display its beauty. No one is too lowly to adorn the gospel.

What it does not mean. It does not endorse slavery as an institution. It tells believers in that hard situation how to live for Christ. The same principles apply to employees: honesty, diligence, respect and trustworthiness make the gospel attractive.

In a sentence. Slaves should submit to their own masters in everything, aiming to please them, not answering back, not stealing on the side, but showing that they can be fully trusted, so that in every way they make the teaching about God our Saviour attractive.

On a Tuesday. Can your employer trust you completely, with time, money and tasks? Let your work this week adorn the gospel.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behind all these instructions lies the gospel. God’s grace has come into view in Christ, offering salvation to people of every kind. That same grace teaches believers to say no to godlessness and worldly cravings and to live sensible, upright and devoted lives in the present age, while they wait for what they long for: the glorious appearing of our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ. He gave himself to free us from all wrongdoing and to make us a cleansed people belonging to him, keen to do good. Titus is to teach these things with full authority and not let anyone dismiss him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Our Great God and Saviour Jesus Christ

By the construction Granville Sharp described, verse 13 names one person — Jesus Christ, our great God and Saviour — closing the letter's alternation of ‘God our Saviour’ and ‘Christ our Saviour’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Grace appeared to all kinds of people — the slave on the same terms as the master (v.11).

Now: Grace is the schoolmaster (v.12), and a people eager for good works is what redemption produces, not its price (v.14).

verseByVerse.quote: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people,

For the grace of God has appeared. Key words. “For” gives the reason for all the instructions of verses 1–10. Godly living is rooted in grace. “Grace” (charis, undeserved favour). “Has appeared” (epephanē, aorist: appeared at a point in history, shone forth, like the sun rising, Luke 1:78–79). The word is related to epiphaneia, “appearing.” Grace appeared in the person of Jesus Christ, in his birth, life, death and resurrection (2 Timothy 1:10; John 1:14, 17).

Bringing salvation. Key words. “Bringing salvation” (sōtērios, saving, salvation-bringing). Grace does not merely offer salvation; it brings it.

For all people. Key words. “For all people” (pasin anthrōpois). In context, all kinds of people: old and young, men and women, slaves and free (vv. 2–10). Grace reaches even slaves, the lowest of society.

Where Christians differ: does grace bring salvation to everyone without exception? Some read this verse as teaching that God’s grace makes salvation available to every individual equally, or even that all will be saved. Verdict: The context shows that “all people” refers to all kinds and classes of people listed in verses 2–10, as in 1 Timothy 2:4–6. Grace has appeared for every category of humanity, without distinction. And grace that “brings salvation” actually saves: it trains those it saves (v. 12) and it redeemed a particular people for God’s own possession (v. 14). This is consistent with definite atonement and effectual grace, while the gospel is still freely offered to everyone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all people will be saved; Scripture teaches eternal judgement for those who reject Christ. Nor does it mean grace is merely an offer awaiting our decision; grace is God’s active, saving power.

In a sentence. For God’s grace has dawned on the world, bringing salvation within reach of every kind of person,

For worship. Thank God that his grace has appeared, not as an idea, but as a person: Jesus Christ, who came to save you.

verseByVerse.quote: training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age,
verseByVerse.commentary:
training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age,

Training us. Key words. “Training” (paideuousa, educating, disciplining, instructing as a child is raised). Grace is not only pardon; it is a teacher. The grace that saves us also trains us. Present tense: a lifelong school. Grace does not make us careless about sin; it makes us hate it.

To renounce ungodliness. Key words. “Renounce” (arnēsamenoi, deny, say no to, reject decisively). Aorist: a decisive break. “Ungodliness” (asebeian, irreverence, lack of regard for God). The root sin: living as if God did not matter.

And worldly passions. Key words. “Worldly passions” (kosmikas epithymias, desires belonging to this world in its rebellion against God): lust, greed, pride, envy (1 John 2:15–17).

And to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives. Key words. Three virtues covering three directions. “Self-controlled” (sōphronōs, sensibly): toward oneself. “Upright” (dikaiōs, justly, righteously): toward others. “Godly” (eusebōs, reverently, devoutly): toward God. A complete life.

In the present age. Key words. “Present age” (nyn aiōni, this age now). Not just in heaven, but here, now, in this fallen world. Grace equips us to live godly lives in an ungodly culture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean grace makes effort unnecessary. Grace trains, and we learn; grace empowers, and we work (Philippians 2:12–13). Nor does it mean we will be perfect in this age; it means we will grow.

In a sentence. and it teaches us to say no to godlessness and the cravings of this world, and to live sensible, upright and devout lives in this present age,

On a Tuesday. What does grace need to train you to say no to this week? Ask God for the strength to say it, and the joy of living for him.

verseByVerse.quote: waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ,

Waiting for our blessed hope. Key words. “Waiting” (prosdechomenoi, expecting, looking forward to, eagerly welcoming). Present tense: continually waiting. “Blessed” (makarian, happy, joyful). “Hope” (elpida): not wishful thinking but certain expectation. Grace looks back to the first appearing (v. 11) and forward to the second (v. 13). Between them we live godly lives (v. 12).

The appearing of the glory. Key words. “Appearing” (epiphaneian), the word used for Christ’s return (1 Timothy 6:14; 2 Timothy 4:1, 8). “Of the glory” (tēs doxēs). Not merely a glorious appearing, but the appearing of the glory itself, the visible display of divine splendour in Christ (Matthew 24:30; 25:31).

Of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. Key words. One of the clearest New Testament statements that Jesus is God. In Greek, one article governs both nouns: “the great God and Savior” (tou megalou theou kai sōtēros hēmōn Iēsou Christou). By a well-known rule of Greek grammar (often called Granville Sharp’s rule), when one article governs two singular personal nouns joined by “and,” both refer to the same person. So Jesus Christ is both “our great God” and “Savior.” Moreover, it is Christ, not the Father, whose appearing the New Testament expects. The same construction appears in 2 Peter 1:1. Other passages also call Jesus God (John 1:1, 18; 20:28; Romans 9:5; Hebrews 1:8).

Where Christians differ: is Jesus called God here? Some, including Jehovah’s Witnesses and some older scholars, translate “the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ,” as referring to two persons, the Father and the Son. Verdict: The grammar, the context, and the New Testament’s consistent expectation of Christ’s (not the Father’s) appearing all support the translation “our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.” This is the reading of most modern translations and of the early Greek church fathers, who spoke Greek as their native language. Christ is fully God, equal with the Father, one God in three persons.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Father and the Son are the same person. They are distinct persons, both fully God. Nor does it mean Christ’s return is secret or partial; it is the public, visible, glorious appearing of God himself in the person of the Son, a single return at the end of the age.

In a sentence. as we wait for the joyful hope we look forward to: the appearing in glory of our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ,

For worship. Worship Jesus Christ today as your great God and Saviour, and long for the day his glory appears.
verseByVerse.note: One of the clearest New Testament statements that Jesus is God.

verseByVerse.quote: who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works. Declare these things; exhort and rebuke with all authority. Let no one disregard you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works. Declare these things; exhort and rebuke with all authority. Let no one disregard you.

Who gave himself for us. Key words. “Gave himself” (edōken heauton): voluntary self-sacrifice (1 Timothy 2:6; Galatians 1:4; 2:20). “For us” (hyper hēmōn, on our behalf, in our place). The heart of the gospel: substitution.

To redeem us from all lawlessness. Key words. “Redeem” (lytrōsētai, ransom, set free by paying a price). The language of buying a slave’s freedom (Mark 10:45; 1 Peter 1:18–19). “All lawlessness” (pasēs anomias): every kind of sin, which is rebellion against God’s law (1 John 3:4). Christ’s death frees us both from sin’s penalty (justification) and from its power (sanctification). Psalm 130:8 says God will redeem Israel from all its iniquities.

And to purify for himself a people. Key words. “Purify” (katharisē, cleanse). Christ died not only to forgive but to make his people clean, holy (Ephesians 5:25–27; Hebrews 9:14).

For his own possession. Key words. “A people for his own possession” (laon periousion, a special people, a treasured possession) echoes God’s words to Israel at Sinai (Exodus 19:5; Deuteronomy 7:6; 14:2). The church, made of Jews and Gentiles, is God’s treasured people, the true Israel (1 Peter 2:9–10). Christ died with a particular people in view, whom he would redeem and make his own. This is definite atonement: his death actually secures the redemption and purification of those for whom he died.

Who are zealous for good works. Key words. “Zealous” (zēlōtēn, eager, enthusiastic, passionate). The goal of redemption is a people burning with eagerness to do good. Good works do not save, but those who are saved are zealous for them (Ephesians 2:10).

Declare these things; exhort and rebuke with all authority. Key words. “Declare” (lalei, speak), as in verse 1. “Exhort” (parakalei, encourage). “Rebuke” (elenche, correct, convict). “With all authority” (meta pasēs epitagēs, with full command). Titus speaks with the authority of God’s word, not his own.

Let no one disregard you. Key words. “Disregard” (periphroneitō, think around, look down on, despise). As with Timothy (1 Timothy 4:12). Titus must not be intimidated, and the Cretans must not ignore him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the zeal for good works earns redemption. Redemption comes first, as Christ’s free gift; zeal for good works follows as its fruit. Nor does “all authority” mean Titus may be harsh or domineering; his authority is the authority of the message.

In a sentence. who gave himself up for us to set us free from every kind of wickedness and to make clean for himself a people who are his very own, eager to do what is good. Teach these things; encourage and correct with full authority. Do not let anyone look down on you.

For worship. Thank Christ that he gave himself for you, to redeem you and make you his own treasured possession. Then ask him to make you zealous for good works today.
verseByVerse.note: “A people for his own possession” echoes God’s words to Israel at Sinai.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>But as for you, teach what accords with sound doctrine.<sup>2</sup>Older men are to be sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled, sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness.<sup>3</sup>Older women likewise are to be reverent in behavior, not slanderers or slaves to much wine. They are to teach what is good,<sup>4</sup>and so train the young women to love their husbands and children,<sup>5</sup>to be self-controlled, pure, working at home, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, that the word of God may not be reviled.<sup>6</sup>Likewise, urge the younger men to be self-controlled.<sup>7</sup>Show yourself in all respects to be a model of good works, and in your teaching show integrity, dignity,<sup>8</sup>and sound speech that cannot be condemned, so that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us.<sup>9</sup>Bondservants are to be submissive to their own masters in everything; they are to be well-pleasing, not argumentative,<sup>10</sup>not pilfering, but showing all good faith, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior.<sup>11</sup>For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people,<sup>12</sup>training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age,<sup>13</sup>waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ,<sup>14</sup>who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works.<sup>15</sup>Declare these things; exhort and rebuke with all authority. Let no one disregard you.

3.title: Heirs of Hope: Conduct in Society and the Gospel's Foundation
3.overview:
The last chapter covers life among unbelieving neighbours (vv. 1–8) and the handling of divisive people (vv. 9–15). Christians are to be good citizens, gentle and courteous to everyone, because they remember what they once were: foolish, enslaved and hateful. What changed them was not their own effort. God our Saviour appeared in kindness and saved us, “not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy”, by the new birth the Spirit gives, so that, justified by grace, we are heirs of eternal life.

Paul then tells Titus to insist on this free grace precisely so that believers will devote themselves to good works. Pointless controversies are to be avoided, a divisive person warned twice and then left alone, and the travelling teachers sent on well supplied.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — He Saved Us, Not Because of Works
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Believers are to respect the governing authorities, be ready to do good, speak evil of no one, avoid fighting, and show gentleness and courtesy to everyone. After all, we too were once foolish, disobedient and deceived, slaves to our desires, full of malice and envy, hating and hated. But when God our Saviour showed his kindness and love, he rescued us, not because of anything good we had done, but because of his mercy, by washing us through new birth and renewing us by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out generously through Jesus Christ. Justified by his grace, we have become heirs with the hope of eternal life. Paul wants Titus to stress this reliable truth, so that believers give themselves to doing good.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace as the Engine of Works

Having excluded even our righteous works from the reason we are saved (v.5), Paul says to insist on that doctrine precisely so that believers devote themselves to good works (v.8). Free grace is not balanced against effort; it drives it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In a province prone to unrest, submission to authorities was the Christian's default posture (v.1; cf. Acts 5:29).

Now: Courtesy toward the ungodly comes from an accurate memory: ‘we ourselves were once’ (v.3).

verseByVerse.quote: Remind them to be submissive to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work, to speak evil of no one, to avoid quarreling, to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers must be submissive to authorities, ready for good works, gentle and courteous to all.

Remind. They had been told. Much of ministry is not new information but recollection.

Submit. As in Romans 13 and 1 Peter 2. Crete was a restless province; a movement suspected of sedition would be crushed.

What it does not mean. Not obedience to anything. The apostles said, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Submission to legitimate authority is the default, not a promise to do wrong when told.

Ready for every good work. Christians should be the people a town is glad to have.

Gentle. Epieikēs: not insisting on the last inch of your rights.

All people. Literally “all meekness to all men”: including the Cretan liars of 1:12, pagan neighbours and Roman officials.

On a Tuesday. How do you speak of politicians you did not vote for? “Speak evil of no one” includes them.

verseByVerse.quote: For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures, passing our days in malice and envy, hated by others and hating one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We were once foolish, disobedient and enslaved, living in malice and hatred.

We ourselves. Not “they”. Paul, the blameless Pharisee (Philippians 3:6), puts himself in the list.

A descent. Foolish, disobedient, deceived; then enslaved, owned by appetites; then malice and envy as the air we breathed; and at the bottom, a society of mutual hatred.

The logic. How do you show courtesy to people who are foolish and hateful? By remembering that the description is yours. Contempt for the ungodly is not cured by trying harder to be patient; it is cured by an accurate memory.

On a Tuesday. When an unbelieving colleague is crude or cruel, remember: that was me, and grace found me there.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God’s kindness appeared, he saved us, not because of our works but by his mercy, through regeneration and renewal by the Spirit.

Appeared. Epiphainō, as at 2:11. Into the hatred of verse 3, kindness shone.

Loving kindness. Philanthrōpia: God as lover of mankind, toward the people just described.

Not even our righteous works. The exclusion is total. Not only bad works, but the best things we have done, are excluded from the reason we are saved.

His own mercy. Mercy is shown to the wretched, not the deserving.

Does baptism give new birth? Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some others read “washing of regeneration” as baptism, linking it with John 3:5 and 1 Peter 3:21. But Paul has just said salvation is not by works done by us, and the washing is joined to “renewal of the Holy Spirit”. The likelier reading is the cleansing the Spirit works in new birth, as promised in Ezekiel 36:25–27, which baptism signs and seals but which does not depend on the water.

Regeneration. A new beginning, not a repaired old one. Both it and renewal are the Spirit’s work, not ours.

For worship. You were not chosen for your potential. You were saved by mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God poured out his Spirit through Christ, so that, justified by grace, we might become heirs of eternal life.

Poured out richly. Pentecost language (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17, 33), now said of Cretan believers. Not rationed by maturity: poured on the people who had been hating one another.

The Trinity at work. The Father saved, by the Spirit, poured out through the Son. Paul cannot describe salvation without all three.

Justified by his grace. The courtroom verdict, on the ground of grace alone.

Heirs. Justification is not the end. An acquitted man walks out owing nothing and owning nothing. We walk out heirs: the court declares us not guilty, and the Father writes us into his will.

Hope. The hope of 1:2, promised before time by the God who cannot lie. The letter has come full circle.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy, and I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works. These things are excellent and profitable for people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is trustworthy, and believers must devote themselves to good works.

Insist on these things. Not mention, but press: the free grace of vv. 4–7.

So that. Here is the surprise. Paul has excluded works from salvation as completely as language allows, and now says: insist on that, so that people will do good works.

Grace the engine. Free grace is not a risk to be balanced with warnings about effort. It drives the effort. Paul’s way to a hard-working church is to hammer justification by grace alone.

Careful. Good works planned, not left to chance. “Devote” can mean practising a trade. Christians are in the business of doing good.

On a Tuesday. Plan one good work this week, by name and by day.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Titus should keep away from pointless arguments about genealogies and disputes about the law, which achieve nothing. Someone who causes divisions should be warned twice and then avoided, since he has turned aside and condemns himself. Paul arranges to meet Titus at Nicopolis for the winter once a replacement arrives, asks him to help Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey, and reminds him that believers must learn to give themselves to good works that meet urgent needs and bear fruit. He closes with greetings and grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Divisive Man, and the Limit on Patience

The factious man (hairetikos) is warned twice, and then left (v.10): restraint and an end, both. Having been told plainly, he stands self-condemned (v.11).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Controversies are ‘unprofitable’ (v.9), set against good works that are ‘profitable’ (v.8).

Now: The letter's refrain lands on something small: see that two travellers lack nothing (vv.13–14).

verseByVerse.quote: But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable and worthless. As for a person who stirs up division, after warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him, knowing that such a person is warped and sinful; he is self-condemned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Avoid foolish controversies, and after two warnings have nothing to do with a divisive person.

Avoid, not win. A church has limited energy. Hours spent on these quarrels are hours not spent on urgent needs (v. 14). The verdict is a ledger: useless here, profitable in v. 8.

What it does not mean. Not that defending the truth is forbidden; Titus must rebuke false teachers (1:13). The test is whether a debate is settled by Scripture and serves godliness, or only feeds curiosity and pride.

Divisive. Hairetikos, root of “heretic”, but here a faction-maker: a man who builds a following around himself. Not someone who disagrees honestly.

Twice, then stop. Restraint: two clear warnings before anything else. And an end: no third. Endless patience with a man splitting a church is no kindness to the church.

Nothing more to do with him. Removal from fellowship (Matthew 18:15–17; 1 Corinthians 5:11–13), still aiming at repentance: “Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother” (2 Thessalonians 3:15).

Self-condemned. Told twice and persisting, he has passed sentence on himself.

verseByVerse.quote: When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, do your best to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there. Do your best to speed Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way; see that they lack nothing. And let our people learn to devote themselves to good works, so as to help cases of urgent need, and not be unfruitful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul gives travel plans and asks Titus to help others, so that believers learn to do good works.

A replacement first. Artemas or Tychicus (Colossians 4:7) will relieve Titus. Paul does not empty a post without filling it.

Nicopolis. “City of Victory”, probably on Greece’s west coast. Paul is free and planning a season’s work, so this letter comes before the imprisonment of 2 Timothy.

Zenas and Apollos. Apollos the Alexandrian (Acts 18:24–28); Zenas a lawyer, Jewish or Roman. Probably the bearers of this letter.

Lack nothing. Travelling teachers depended on churches. Sending them off short was failure.

Learn. Good works do not come naturally. “Urgent need” is the emergency in front of you. A fruitless tree is not neutral; it is failing at being a tree.

On a Tuesday. The letter’s great refrain lands on something small: give the missionary on furlough a car for the week.
verseByVerse.note: Nicopolis was probably the city of that name on the west coast of Greece. Apollos was the gifted teacher from Alexandria.

verseByVerse.quote: All who are with me send greetings to you. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul closes with greetings and grace.

Those who love us in the faith. After a letter full of people who did not, Paul greets those bound to him by holding the same truth.

You all. Plural. A letter to one man was read to the churches: elders, older women, young wives, slaves, and perhaps the divisive man with two warnings still to come.

Grace. The letter’s first word (1:4), its argument (2:11; 3:7), and its last.

A textual note. Many manuscripts add “Amen”, as scribes often did at the end of letters. It is probably not original.

For worship. To an island known for lying and disorder, Paul sent a short letter about decent leaders, good behaviour and grace. On the evidence of the centuries that followed, it was enough.
